title: SIU reopens separate probes into two Brantford deaths in move called 'exceptional'
subtitle: The decision to reopen an investigation is 'very rare,' according to Ian Scott, who led the SIU for five years ending in 2013. Two in one week in a small city even more remarkable
article: For the second time in less than a week Tuesday, Ontario's provincial police watchdog reopened an investigation into a police-linked death in Brantford, a move one former head of the agency called "singular, and even exceptional."

On Jan. 20, 2009, Oakville's Benjamin Wood, 32, fell through the ice on the Grand River in Brantford after scuffling with the local police. He later died of hypothermia and drowning, according to the coroner.
The provincial Special Investigations Unit looked into the case at the time but found "no criminal liability" on behalf of the Brantford Police Service.
But on Tuesday, six years to the day after Wood died, the SIU announced it was restarting the probe based on "materially new information coming to light."

The decision to reopen an investigation is "very rare," according to Ian Scott, who led the SIU for five years ending in 2013. "The vast majority of the time, the investigations are completed, they're reviewed by the director and then a decision is made. And that's the end of it," Mr. Scott said.
Making this case even stranger is that the SIU reopened a separate police-linked death investigation in Brantford just last week.

In August 2010, Brantford Police Constable Adam Hill shot and killed 18-year-old Evan Jones in his own home. The SIU cleared Const. Hill at the time. But on Jan. 14, director Tony Loparco announced that "materially new information" had come to light in that case, too, prompting the agency to reopen the probe.
The SIU won't comment further while the new investigations are underway. A call to the Brantford police was not immediately returned Tuesday.
But Mr. Scott said the reopening of two different probes involving one small police force in a single week was "singular and even exceptional."
"This is a once-in-a-lifetime situation," he said. "Just think about it, Brantford's just not that big."
According to SIU records, the agency only investigated two police-involved deaths involving the Brantford Police Service between 2008-09 and 2012-13. Both of those are now being looked at again.

To reopen an investigation, Mr. Scott said, the SIU would need to see new evidence that could significantly affect the outcome of a case, such as a new witness, or new testimony from an old one. During his time at the agency, Mr. Scott reopened a handful of probes, including several involving officers at the G20 in Toronto.

According to the SIU's original summary of the Wood case, a Brantford police officer followed a set of shoe prints from a stolen car to the bank of the Grand River near the Brantford Casino in the early hours of a cold winter morning. He found Wood standing on the river and asked him to get off the ice. Wood approached the officer. The two fought and Wood ran back over the bank.

"Other officers responded and pleaded with Mr. Wood to get off the ice," the SIU said at the time. "Mr. Wood would not do so, but instead walked and then ran out into the centre of the ice-covered river. He fell through the ice and drowned."

In the case of Mr. Jones, according to the SIU's original investigation, police responded to a domestic dispute. They found the teen on his porch holding two knifes. When he went back inside and refused to drop the blades, an officer pepper-sprayed him. When Mr. Jones responded by tossing the knives, one after the other, in the officers' direction, Const. Hill shot him four times.
